an1.248:1.1: They were merchants from Ukkalā (modern Odisha on the Bay of Bengal) who offered the first meal to the Buddha after his awakening ([pli-tv-kd1:4.2.1]()). Their spiritual attainments are noted at [an6.119]()–20. Tapussa also appears at [an9.41]().
an1.249:1.1: His given name was Sudatta, but he is usually known by the sobriquet Anāthapiṇḍika, “feeder of the poor”. Renowned as the foremost of benefactors, Anāthapiṇḍika appears in over twenty discourses in the Saṁyutta and Aṅguttara Nikāyas, discussing matters such as generosity, guarding the mind, and the development of meditation. The story of his conversion is recorded in the Vinaya ([pli-tv-kd16:4.1.1]()). He is well known for his offering of the monastery at which the Buddha most often stayed. His death and return are recounted in [mn143]().
an1.250:1.1: The householder Citta, often identified as “of Macchikāsaṇḍa”,  was a chief lay disciple ([an2.132:1.2]()). His boldness and intelligence mark his distinctive personality. Likely he was born under the asterism Citrā (the star Spica), a manifestation of Agni (see Pāṇini 4.3.34, _vārttika_ 1). The primordial myth of the asterism attributes to it the power to enable one of lower status (the titans) to challenge those of higher status, the gods (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.1.2.13–17). Citta the householder is likewise noted for his brilliant insight that surpasses the monks ([sn41.1]()); moreover, on several occasions in his presence the most junior monastic surpasses the senior (eg. [sn41.2]()).
an1.251:1.1: His skill in attracting and managing a large following is featured in [an8.23]() and [an8.24](). He is often paired with Citta as examplars of male lay followers (eg. [sn17.23:1.4]()).
an1.252:1.1: Mahānāma was the brother of Anuruddha and Ānanda ([pli-tv-kd17:1.1.3]()) which, according to the commentary, makes the Buddha his cousin. He remained in the lay life as a devoted and generous follower, keenly interested in developing his practice. The early texts do not record any occasion of his awakening. However, the commentarial claim that he was a once-returner is supported by passages such as [sn55.22:2.3]() and [sn55.21:3.6]() that suggest he was indeed a noble disciple.
an1.253:1.1: The Uggas were one of the leading _khattiya_ clans of Vesālī. Ugga’s giving is exemplified at [an5.44]().
an1.254:1.1: His name varies between Ugga and Uggata; I use Uggata for clarity. He is praised at [an8.22](), and converses with the Buddha at [sn35.125]().
an1.255:1.1: Of the same clan as Ambaṭṭha of [dn3]().
